slides.title: Readiness means try now, not a whole request is ready
keyPoints: One slow client must not stop all other clients
Keep descriptors nonblocking in the event loop
Retain partial protocol state between callbacks
slides.narration: A readiness loop waits for endpoints that may make progress and then attempts their operations. The notification does not promise a complete message, a complete write, or permanent readiness. Another thread or event can change the state before the handler runs. Nonblocking descriptors let the handler discover would-block and return to servicing other connections. A blocking read for the rest of one client's request can stall every other client sharing the loop. The price of efficient waiting is explicit state: buffered input, parsing position, output offset, close status, and any deadline must survive across callbacks.

slides.title: A partial write advances an offset, not the whole response
keyPoints: Keep the unsent suffix in owned storage
Advance only by the reported positive count
Finish when the offset reaches the response length
slides.narration: This deterministic write-progress model starts with hello and supplied accepted counts of two, one, and two. After the first step only he has been accepted; the next starts at offset two and adds l; the final step adds lo. The output reports sent equals hello and pending equals zero. No socket or timing claim is involved. The point is the state that a real nonblocking handler must preserve across writes. Starting from the beginning after partial progress duplicates bytes, while discarding the response after the first call loses its suffix. The owning response must outlive every borrowed pointer used for an attempted write.

slides.title: A busy connection can monopolize a correct loop
keyPoints: Draining work affects fairness as well as throughput
A service budget can return control to other clients
Edge-triggered designs need a continuation plan
slides.narration: In this scheduling model, busy client A has eight work items ready and client B has one. Draining all of A first puts B in ninth position. A two-item service budget puts B in third position instead. Both schedules complete the same nine items, but the delay seen by B differs. These are modeled service positions, not measured milliseconds. In a real edge-triggered reactor, stopping before would-block needs a deliberate continuation mechanism; otherwise already-buffered work might never produce a new edge. Fairness therefore requires coordinating handler budgets with the readiness mode, rather than simply breaking every loop early.

slides.title: Would-block, EOF, and error require different transitions
keyPoints: Would-block: retain state and wait for progress
EOF: no more input bytes will arrive
Other error: apply the failure policy
slides.narration: The source workshop assigns minus one a special modeled would-block meaning, but a real read returning minus one requires inspecting errno. A zero result on a stream indicates EOF, while a positive count adds valid bytes. Those cases must remain distinct. If a temporary lack of data closes the connection, valid clients are dropped. If EOF is treated as temporary emptiness forever, dead connections remain in the loop. A framing layer adds one more question: does EOF occur between complete frames or inside an unfinished one? The answer determines graceful completion versus truncation.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
keyPoints: In real read calls, -1 requires inspecting errno; this model uses -1 only as a named would-block event. Treating every -1 as would-block loses real errors.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Treat every nonpositive result as EOF. A live connection is closed when it merely has no bytes ready now.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Distinguish success, EOF, would-block, interruption, and permanent errors according to the API. Return control to the event loop on would-block.

keyPoints: Would-block means the operation cannot make immediate progress; EOF means the stream has ended. Keeping them separate prevents a temporary lack of data from closing a connection. slides.title: Chapter 53 — Event-Driven I/O
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: An event-driven server keeps many connection state machines in a smaller number of execution threads.
Instead of blocking one thread per idle connection, it waits for readiness and advances the corresponding state only as far as current I/O permits.
This trades simple sequential control flow for explicit state, buffers, and scheduling policy.
Readiness is not completion.

keyPoints: An event loop waits, dispatches ready connections, performs bounded work, updates interest masks, and handles timers and shutdown.

Register write readiness only when output remains pending; an idle socket is often writable and can otherwise wake the loop continuously.
For edge-triggered operation, stopping before EAGAIN for fairness requires an explicit rescheduling strategy so that remaining work is not forgotten while waiting for a new edge.

slides.title: Level and edge notifications create different obligations
keyPoints: Level triggering reports a condition that remains true
Edge triggering reports relevant changes
An edge handler normally drains until would-block
slides.narration: Suppose four bytes are buffered and a handler reads only two. A level-triggered readiness mechanism can continue reporting that readable data remains. With edge-triggered notification, another event is not guaranteed merely because the remaining two bytes are still there. The usual receive-side rule is to continue reading until would-block or EOF. The source Linux example sends ping through a local socket pair and drains it in small chunks, making that obligation visible. Readiness does not itself consume bytes. The handler must also enforce buffer bounds and protocol limits while draining, rather than accepting unlimited input in pursuit of EAGAIN.

question.prompt: Why might reading only one small chunk after an edge leave a connection stuck?
question.answer: Existing unread bytes may not create another edge. The handler needs to drain them or arrange an explicit continuation.

slides.title: Closure notification does not erase the last bytes
keyPoints: Data and peer shutdown can be observable together
Drain valid bytes before concluding input is finished
Keep half-close separate from total object destruction
slides.narration: A peer can send its final response and then close its sending direction. The receiver may observe both readable data and a closure condition during one event cycle. Closing immediately on the notification can discard the final bytes. The local epoll example demonstrates this by sending ping and half-closing, then reading through EOF. Half-close means one direction has ended; the application may still need to finish pending output in the other direction. The state machine must decide when no further input is possible, whether a frame is complete, and when all owned resources can finally be released.

slides.title: select, poll, and epoll change the waiting interface
keyPoints: select uses descriptor sets and platform limits
poll supplies an array of descriptor events
epoll retains registered interest in a Linux kernel object
slides.narration: These interfaces all help one thread wait for I/O across multiple descriptors, but they organize the request differently. select uses descriptor sets and has limits tied to that representation. poll passes an array describing desired events. Linux epoll retains registered interests and returns events through its own descriptor. Choosing epoll does not automatically make every operation nonblocking, allocate connection state, or solve fairness. Those remain application responsibilities. Compare portability, expected connection counts, registration changes, and the available readiness modes. Keep protocol handlers separate enough that changing the waiting interface does not require rewriting message validation.

question.prompt: Which responsibilities remain even after switching from poll to epoll?
question.answer: Nonblocking operation handling, per-connection state, framing, ownership, bounds, fairness, and shutdown. The readiness API handles only part of the design.

slides.title: Writable interest should follow pending output
keyPoints: Most connected sockets can be writable much of the time
Continuous writable notifications can spin the loop
Enable interest while bytes remain, disable it when drained
slides.narration: A service that always subscribes to writable events may repeatedly wake even when it has nothing to send. That consumes CPU without completing useful work. A common policy enables writable interest when the output queue becomes nonempty and removes it after the queue drains. If a write would block, the unsent suffix remains owned by the connection until later readiness. The queue must also have a size bound: a fast producer and slow client can otherwise retain unlimited memory. This connects event registration to application state rather than treating readiness subscriptions as a one-time setup choice.

question.prompt: Why can a loop show high CPU use while completing no requests?
question.answer: It may repeatedly process irrelevant readiness, such as writable notifications with no pending output, or spin on would-block instead of waiting.

slides.title: Descriptor reuse makes stale event identity dangerous
keyPoints: A descriptor number is not a permanent connection identity
Remove registration and end borrowed uses before destruction
Generation identifiers can distinguish replacement connections
slides.narration: After one connection closes, the operating system may reuse its descriptor integer for another connection. A delayed task that stores only the integer can then act on the wrong peer. The problem is lifetime and identity, not whether integers compare correctly. Event data should refer to connection state whose lifetime remains valid, or include a generation scheme that lets the program reject stale work. Shutdown must coordinate unregistering interest, pending callbacks, worker jobs, and final closure. A pointer inside an event record is also only a borrow unless the design explicitly keeps its target alive.

slides.title: Test event sequences, not only one successful exchange
keyPoints: Fragment input and restrict write progress
Combine final data with EOF
Force temporary would-block without closure
Verify pending-state cleanup and fair continuation
slides.narration: A reliable event handler should survive several schedules for the same logical conversation. Split the header across reads, make writes accept short prefixes, deliver final bytes with EOF, and insert would-block between successful steps. Compare the completed message and the remaining state after every event. The portable models make such sequences deterministic, while the local socket fixture checks the real Linux receive mechanism. Neither is a complete production server. Tests for resource limits, cancellation, timeouts, output backpressure, and stale events must grow with the application's contract rather than being assumed from a passing ping exchange.
